You are being evaluated on Continual-ARC, a lifelong stream of ARC-style grid puzzles.
Each puzzle instance has a task id and a test input grid. Tasks recur across the
stream with fresh inputs. Each instance is a separate conversation: the next one
starts without this one's messages.

On every message you must choose exactly one action and put it as a JSON object
on the last line of your reply:
  {"action": "submit", "grid": [[0, 1, 2], [3, 4, 5]]}   submit an output grid
  {"action": "request_demos"}                            ask for one more demonstration pair for this task
  {"action": "finish"}                                   end the instance, once it is over
Grids are lists of rows; cells are integers 0-9; dimensions are 1-30.

Each demo request returns one more input-output pair of the task, up to the demo cap shown
with the input.

Scoring: an instance you solve costs 1 for each wrong submission and 1 for
each demo request. An instance is over when a submission is correct or when the attempt
cap is reached, and one that ends unsolved costs the whole budget, 16, however
many submissions and demo requests it used. Feedback on a submission is only
correct/incorrect. There is no way to abandon an instance, and finish is refused until
the instance is over. Each instance is scored on its own, and lower cost is better.

# Continual-ARC task notes

## task-dbb85d02: horizontal paired bars
Observed task family: mostly uniform background with separated horizontal motifs. In simple cases, preserve bars and recolor only contiguous background tail cells to their right with color 1 when target bar ends before the grid edge; full-width bars unchanged. Patterned motifs need context: only select the corresponding bars identified by the repeated motif, not every partial bar. Examples include changes to specific tails in the lower repeated motifs. Generalize cautiously and inspect motif structure.

## task-766879a9: aligned panels and shared-color coincidence mask
Verified solved test (2026-10-21) after two demos. Input consists of two equal-sized noisy panels separated by a uniform divider row or column. Each panel uses two colors, with exactly one color shared between both panels. Output is the cellwise agreement mask for the shared color: dimensions equal one panel; fill output with the shared color, except output 3 wherever the aligned cell in BOTH panels is that shared color. Compare aligned coordinates directly; do not reverse/flip panels; exclude divider.

Evidence from demos: horizontal demo 1 had divider color 4, upper palette {1,5}, lower palette {2,5}; shared color=5, output 9x21 filled with 5 and 3 exactly where both corresponding cells were 5. Vertical demo 2 had divider color 7, left palette {8,5}, right palette {8,1}; shared=8, output 24x7 filled with 8 and 3 where both aligned panel cells were 8. Solved test had divider row of 4s, top palette {6,2}, bottom palette {5,2}; shared=2. Output 10x15 had base 2, with 3 at the positions where corresponding cells in top 10x15 and bottom 10x15 panels both equaled 2. Only the first 10 rows above the divider and rows 11-20 below it are panels; row 10 is divider.

The task is robust to divider orientation and differing panel-specific colors. To solve: identify the separator; split into equal panels; find their common palette color (not divider); output panel size with shared-color base and mark 3 only at intersections where both aligned inputs equal the shared color. Avoid returning the panel itself or merely converting one panel's foreground.

Additional verified test (2026-10-21): 9x23 input with a full-height divider column of 5 at column 12; left 9x11 panel palette {4,6}, right 9x11 panel palette {1,6}, so shared color=6. Output is 9x11 filled with 6, with 3 only at aligned coordinates where both panels have 6. In this test the only such coordinate was row 5, column 5 (1-based). This confirmed the vertical split interpretation and exact coincidence rule.

Additional verified test (2026-10-21): 29x2 input, with divider row [0,0] at row 15. The upper 14x2 panel uses colors {8,1}; lower 14x2 panel (rows 16-29) uses {4,1}; shared color=1. Output is 14x2, base 1, with 3 exactly at aligned positions where both panels contain 1. Correct output (1-based positions marked 3): r2 c2; r3 c2; r5 c2; r8 c1; r10 c1; r12 c2; r13 c2. Exact output: [[1,1],[1,3],[1,3],[1,1],[1,3],[1,1],[1,1],[3,1],[1,1],[3,1],[1,1],[1,3],[1,3],[1,1]]. My first answer was wrong because it marked some individual 1s without verifying the aligned cell in the other panel, and marked both cells in a row where only column 2 matched. Reminder: a cell is 3 only if BOTH aligned panel cells equal the shared color; a shared-color cell in just one panel remains base color.

Additional verified test (2026-10-21): task-766879a9, input 2x19, with zero divider column at c10. The two 2x9 panels are columns 1-9 and 11-19. Left palette {6,7}, right palette {4,6}, shared color=6. Output is 2x9 filled with 6; mark 3 only when both corresponding cells are 6. Only matching coordinate was output row 2, column 4, so output [[6,6,6,6,6,6,6,6,6],[6,6,6,3,6,6,6,6,6]]. This validates the shared-color coincidence rule for a very narrow horizontal split with a single-column divider.

Additional verified test (2026-10-21): task-766879a9, input 29x2, with row 15 [8,8] as the divider. The top 14x2 panel uses {9,7}, and bottom 14x2 panel (rows 16-29) uses {7,5}; shared color=7. Output is 14x2, base 7, with 3 exactly where aligned cells in both panels are 7. Correct output: [[7,3],[3,7],[3,7],[7,3],[3,7],[7,3],[7,3],[3,3],[3,7],[3,3],[7,3],[7,3],[3,7],[7,7]]. A first attempt incorrectly marked the final output cell (row 14, col 2) as 3; the aligned upper cell is 9, so it must remain 7. This reinforces: only mark 3 where both aligned panel cells equal the shared color, including at the panel edge.

Additional verified test (2026-10-21): task-766879a9, input 15x14 with a horizontal divider row of 9s at row 8. The top 7x14 panel uses {8,1}; the bottom 7x14 panel (rows 9-15) uses {7,1}; shared color=1. Compare aligned coordinates directly, indexing each panel from its own first row. None of the 1-cells coincide at the same panel-relative row and column, so the correct output is a 7x14 grid filled entirely with 1 (no 3s). My first submission incorrectly marked output row 4, column 2 due to a misalignment/visual comparison; after correcting the aligned-coordinate check, the all-1 output was accepted. Lesson: do not infer a match from nearby/repeated 1s—verify the same column in the corresponding row of both panels. The task can have zero coincidence cells.

Additional verified test (2026-10-21): task-766879a9, 17x29 input, vertical divider column 15 (value 0), panels are 17x14 at cols 1-14 and 16-29. Left palette {9,2}, right palette {5,9}, shared color=9. Output is 17x14 with base 9 and 3 only where left panel cell and corresponding right-panel cell are both 9. Accepted output:
[[9,9,3,9,9,9,9,9,9,9,9,9,9,9],[9,9,9,9,9,9,9,9,9,9,3,9,9,9],[9,9,3,9,9,9,9,9,9,3,9,9,9,9],[3,9,9,9,9,9,9,9,9,9,9,9,9,9],[9,9,9,9,9,9,9,9,9,9,9,9,9,9],[9,9,9,9,9,3,9,9,9,9,9,9,9,9],[9,9,9,3,9,9,9,9,9,9,9,9,9,9],[9,9,9,9,9,9,9,9,9,9,9,9,9,9],[9,3,9,9,9,9,9,9,9,9,9,9,9,3],[9,9,9,9,9,9,9,9,9,9,3,9,9,9],[9,9,9,9,9,9,9,9,9,9,9,9,9,9],[9,9,9,9,9,9,9,9,9,9,9,9,9,9],[9,9,9,9,9,9,9,9,9,9,9,9,9,9],[3,9,9,9,9,9,9,9,9,9,9,9,9,9],[9,9,9,9,9,9,9,9,9,9,9,9,9,9],[9,9,9,9,9,9,9,9,9,9,9,9,9,9],[9,9,9,9,9,9,9,9,9,9,9,9,9,9]].
Important failure lesson: do not infer output marks merely from right-panel deviations or approximately aligned visual patterns; mark 3 only at exact same panel-relative coordinate where both values are 9. Earlier wrong attempts repeatedly misindexed row 2 (mark is c11, not c10), row 3 (marks c3 and c10), and row 10 (mark c11). To avoid drift, use 1-based indexing and validate each candidate against both panels before submitting; right-panel 9 candidates for this input are: r1c3, r2c11, r3c3/c10, r4c1, r6c6, r7c4, r9c2/c14, r10c11, r14c1. These are the complete set of output 3 coordinates (all other output cells remain 9).
